rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the full elution window without severe risk of truncation. This gives a first read on whether peaks are unretained early, bunched in the middle, or still eluting in the high-organic hold.

All 10 peaks eluted with excellent resolution in a much smaller effective window, so trim the gradient to roughly bracket the observed elution range and cut high-organic excess. This should keep all peaks in-gradient while reducing run time and testing whether the broad scout can be compressed without losing the critical 6/7 separation.

The scout already has full resolution, so the main opportunity is reducing time; halve tG while keeping the broad window to see how much the critical mid-cluster compresses. This directly measures slope sensitivity of the closest pairs and may improve CRF if resolution remains acceptable.

At tG 10 the 5/6/7 cluster is over-compressed, while tG 20 had ample resolution but unnecessary time, so test an intermediate slope. This should recover separation of the critical pair while likely keeping the run short enough to beat or approach the current best CRF.

The main tradeoff is now centered on the 6/7 pair: tG 14 is close but still slightly under-resolved, while tG 20 is more than enough but slower. A small increase to tG 16 should improve the critical resolution with minimal time penalty and may reach the top CRF.

The 6/7 pair is only weakly improved by slope, so temperature is the best lever left to test selectivity near the current optimum. Dropping T slightly should modestly increase retention and may reorder or spread the critical cluster without much time penalty.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity in the critical cluster, so test the opposite direction at the same near-optimal slope. A modest increase to 45 C may improve the 6/7 region enough to raise the resolution term while preserving the short run.

Keep the near-optimal slope and temperature but slightly narrow the upper end of the gradient window to alter selectivity in the crowded mid-region without major time cost. Since the last peak eluted well before the end of the gradient, lowering phi1 a bit should still elute all compounds while testing whether the 6/7 pair can be improved.

Narrowing the upper gradient limit from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical 6/7 pair, so continue in the same direction with a small additional reduction in phi1. The last peak is still comfortably within the programmed gradient, making this a low-risk selectivity refinement that could push the minimum resolution higher.

The 0.90 upper limit improved selectivity, and at 14 min the resolution term is very high but still just below perfect; slightly steepening the gradient may retain enough separation while reducing late retention. This tests whether the better phi window can support a shorter run than 14 min without collapsing the 6/7 pair as badly as the broader 0.95 window did.

The slope–window combination at 0.05–0.90 and 14 min is strongest so far, and temperature remains the main untested selectivity lever around it. A cooler setting than 35 C may shift the crowded 5/6/7 region differently than the broad-window runs did and could turn the near-perfect 1.36 minimum resolution into a fully resolved pattern.

The best region is clearly around 0.05–0.90, 14 min, 40 C; with the first peak still reasonably retained, a small increase in phi0 is a clean way to narrow the gradient window further and probe selectivity in the crowded mid-cluster. This may improve the critical pair without much effect on total runtime.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved the near-optimal method, so combine that gain with the earlier benefit from lowering phi1. This further narrows the active gradient window around the actual elution range and may push the critical 6/7 pair over the threshold without incurring a time penalty.

CRF is already at the maximum, so this is a confirmatory refinement to see whether the gradient can be narrowed a bit further from the low-organic end while keeping all peaks fully resolved. The first peak is still comfortably retained, so increasing phi0 may preserve the plateau optimum and reveal whether the method is robust or over-trimmed.

You are on a CRF plateau, so continue mapping its edge by raising phi0 one more step while holding the successful upper limit and slope. This checks whether the earliest peak is approaching the unretained region and how far the low-organic end can be trimmed without sacrificing full resolution.

The low-end trim plateau appears to top out at phi0 0.10–0.15, so now probe the upper edge by lowering phi1 one step from the successful 0.85 method. This should reveal whether the window can be narrowed further while keeping the late peak in-gradient and preserving the fully resolved mid-cluster.

The best plateau includes phi0 0.10–0.15 at phi1 0.85, and lowering phi1 to 0.80 at phi0 0.15 kept full resolution with only a tiny time penalty. Testing phi0 0.10 with phi1 0.80 maps the remaining corner of that plateau and may recover the last few tenths of a minute while staying at the CRF maximum.

The CRF maximum spans at least phi0 0.10–0.15 with phi1 0.85, and phi0 0.15 gave the shortest fully optimal run so far. Testing phi1 0.90 at the same phi0 checks the adjacent plateau edge and may keep the perfect score with a slightly earlier last peak.

You have established a robust CRF=1 plateau at 14 min, so the best remaining opportunity is to test whether that narrower, better-selective window can tolerate a slightly steeper gradient. This probes whether runtime can be reduced while preserving full resolution, especially for the persistent 6/7 critical pair.

Since 12 min was too steep and 14 min already reaches CRF 1.000, test the opposite direction to define robustness on the shallow side. This should confirm whether the perfect-score region extends to longer gradients and whether the critical 6/7 pair gains extra margin without invoking a time penalty.

You already have CRF 1.000, so use remaining budget to probe robustness of one optimal composition under a mild temperature increase. This tests whether temperature can preserve the maximum score on the plateau or sharply degrade the key 6/7 separation, helping define a robust final operating space.

Temperature clearly affects the critical pair strongly, so use a remaining run to test the other optimal-composition point at a mild decrease in T. This helps bracket robustness around the CRF=1 methods and checks whether phi0 0.15 is less temperature-sensitive than phi0 0.10.

With the optimum fixed at 40 C and strong temperature sensitivity established on both sides, use a remaining run to map the upper-temperature failure edge more explicitly. This will show how sharply selectivity collapses beyond 45 C for an otherwise optimal composition and further define method robustness limits.

One last robustness check on the other CRF=1 composition will complete the temperature map around the optimal window. This tests whether phi0 0.15 is any more tolerant to elevated temperature than phi0 0.10 while preserving the already established best method family.

For the final run, map the remaining untested corner near the optimal plateau by combining the more aggressive low- and high-end trims at the known best temperature and slope. This checks whether the window can be narrowed further while retaining full resolution, but the established best methods remain 0.10–0.85–14–40 and 0.15–0.85–14–40.
